extracted.intended_audience: aspiring TV writers / people who pitch sitcom ideas (novices and non-industry pitch-givers)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on what makes a viable sitcom premise and how to pitch it — emphasising character-driven ideas, sustainable dynamics, and realistic expectations about the TV creative/process. Aimed at people who have informal 'my life/work is a sitcom' ideas and want to shape them into sellable concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the characters first
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find who the characters are and what about the dynamics between them is interesting, fresh, and could sustain stories week after week. Only after you understand the characters should you choose the best setting to put them in. (From the post: 'Start with the characters first. What about the dynamics between them are interesting, fresh, and could sustain stories week after week? And then, what is the best setting to put them in?')

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters and relationships (especially under pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters and relationships, absolutely. Characters and relationships under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often arises from the interactions and relationships among people — particularly when those relationships are tested or put under pressure. Emphasise relational dynamics as the engine for episode-to-episode stories rather than isolated gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should serve characters, not the other way around
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot should serve characters, not the other way around.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus story ideas so they reveal or challenge the characters; avoid building plots that exist solely to showcase a crazy concept without grounding in character motivation or development. (Brian Fies anecdote: Star Trek staff preferred stories about characters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: A workplace/occupation alone is not a premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Just because you sell lamps, or work in a real estate office, or a Costco, ... this does not mean you have the premise for a sitcom. You have the premise for a work location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a distinct job or quirky co-workers gives you setting/color but not the sustaining dramatic/comedic engine. Don't pitch 'we work here and funny stuff happens' as the show — you need character relationships and dynamics that justify recurring episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated 'hilarious incidents' are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Most pitches list a few hilarious incidents (single anecdotes) as proof of a sitcom idea, but those one-off stories do not constitute a show premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few funny workplace anecdotes (e.g., the sugar-in-coffee story) do not translate into a series unless they point to deeper character relationships and repeatable conflicts; avoid relying on anecdotal gags as the core pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting novelty is a plus but not required
rubrics_metrics.description: One that hasn’t been seen before is a plus but not imperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A unique setting can help a pitch stand out, but originality of location is secondary to interesting, sustainable character dynamics. Familiar settings (bars, offices) can work if the characters and relationships are compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some premises are hard to sell / avoid certain sensitive concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Madcap terrorist cells probably won’t fly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that certain subject matters or extreme concepts are difficult to sell or tastefully handle in sitcom form. Consider marketability and audience sensitivity when shaping a premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the creative process and realistic credit expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: People who pitch think they have done the fundamental heavy lifting and expect a 'created by' credit after writers take the setting and fill it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you pitch, know that writers/producers develop characters, plots, and navigate the pilot process; simply providing a setting or anecdote typically doesn't entitle the pitcher to creative credit. Pitch with realistic expectations about what constitutes a usable idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insider-only or niche humor that won’t play broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Trouble is, only academics would get the jokes, and half of them claim they don't watch TV...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the comic material depends on a small, insider audience, it will likely not translate to a broad sitcom audience. Aim for humor that is accessible enough for general viewers while retaining distinctive voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: For any genre show, emphasize characters over high-concept gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: When freelancers pitched Star Trek, nearly all pitched alien/ship concepts and not the show's characters — but the staff wanted stories about characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes beyond sitcoms: even in high-concept or genre series, decision-makers prefer stories that foreground character choices and development. Frame pitches around how the concept reveals or challenges character rather than the gadget/monster/concept itself.
